lessons.title: Three supply numbers
lessons.content:
# Three supply numbers

A tokenomics poster usually prints one integer in a giant font. That integer is almost never the one that would change a decision. Supply is three numbers that can disagree by an order of magnitude, plus a policy about who is allowed to change them. Treating the giant font as “the supply” is how people buy a slogan.

This academy will not assign a pair and will not narrate a candle into homework. The job of this course is to make supply into arithmetic you can date-stamp.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to name max supply, totalSupply, and circulating as three different machines, and refuse a pie chart that does not say which integer it used.

## Max, total, circulating

**Max supply** is a ceiling the author claims: a constant in code, a comment, or a sentence on a website. Sometimes there is no ceiling. A ceiling in a whitepaper that is not enforced in the contract is a wish.

**Total supply** (`totalSupply` on a BEP-20) is the integer the contract currently reports as existing units, usually after mint and burn. It is the only one of the three that a read function will give you without a story. Date-stamp it. It can move.

**Circulating** is a subtraction someone performed: total, minus burns they consider dead, minus locks they consider frozen, minus “team” wallets they consider not-for-sale. Two honest people can get two circulating numbers from the same holder list because they disagree about what still can `transfer`. Circulating is a **memo**, not a field.

Worked numbers. Suppose a page says max 1,000,000,000, the contract’s `totalSupply` reads 800,000,000, and a dashboard prints circulating 200,000,000. You now have three objects. The 200 million is only as good as the list of wallets it subtracted. If a labelled “locked” address sent tokens yesterday, the dashboard is theatre.

## Who may change which integer

Max changes if the contract allows a raise, if there is a proxy and an admin upgrades the ceiling, or if there never was a ceiling. Total changes when `mint` or `burn` (or a rebase) runs. Circulating changes when labelled wallets move, when a locker pays out, when a pair is seeded, and when a dashboard author changes a formula.

A pie chart without addresses is a drawing. Demand the three integers, the date, and the subtraction list. If the author cannot produce them, you do not have tokenomics. You have a poster.

Control is a person. `owner()`, a minter role, a proxy admin — these are addresses. “The community” is not an address. If mint still exists, totalSupply is a policy instrument, not a law of nature.

## Crystal Stones as a read, not a hymn

Crystal Stones, as this academy teaches it, is a BEP-20 on BNB Smart Chain, chain ID **56**, at `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`. Older materials may print figures near **135,000,000** total and **104,100,000** circulating. Those are historical marketing numbers until they match what you read on the day you care.

The homework is: bookmark an explorer, paste the address from paper you wrote yourself, call `totalSupply`, write the integer and the date. Match means consistency on that integer. Match is not a mine, not a buy order, and not tuition. Intermediate checkout is **$10 USDT BEP-20** on the academy page. Gas on BSC is **BNB**. Staff never ask for a seed.

## Worked refusal

A chat posts “supply is 104 million, tiny float, load the bag.” You ask: max, total, circulating, date, subtraction list, and whether mint still runs. If the reply is a screenshot of a pie with no 0x, you refuse the sentence. You still do not have a trade from this school. You have a better question.

TABLE
Integer | What it is | How it lies
Max | Claimed ceiling | Whitepaper only; proxy can raise it
totalSupply | Contract’s current units | Stale if you screenshot last year
Circulating | Someone’s subtraction | “Locked” wallets that still transfer
Dashboard float | A UI rounding | Hides mint and unlocks
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
THREE INTEGERS (write the date)
max          1,000,000,000   <- code, comment, or wish
totalSupply    800,000,000   <- read on the explorer
circulating    200,000,000   <- memo: total minus ???
If ??? is missing, circulating is a drawing.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rails: Intermediate is $10 USDT BEP-20 on academy checkout — not Crystal Stones token, not a chat 0x. Crystal Stones at `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on BSC (chain ID 56) is verify-only. Gas on BSC is BNB. Staff never ask for a seed, key, 2FA, or remote control. This course will not tell you to buy anything.
ENDNOTE

## How a dashboard invents circulating

Circulating is almost never a Solidity getter. Dashboards subtract addresses they have labelled: vesting contracts, “team”, “locked LP”, “ecosystem”. Labels go stale. A wallet tagged locked can still `transfer`. A locker can `release`. If you cannot name the subtraction list with 0x addresses and a date, you do not have circulating. You have a caption.

Worked integers. `totalSupply` reads 800,000,000. A slide says 200,000,000 circulating. That implies 600,000,000 is “not circulating.” Name those 600 million: which contracts, which EOAs, which cliffs. If the answer is a colour on a pie, circulating is art. If a labelled “locked” EOA moves 10 million tomorrow, yesterday’s circulating was a costume.

## Max, cap, and the function that ignores both

Max supply on a poster is a wish unless `mint` reverts when `totalSupply + amount > cap`. Some contracts have a `cap` variable the owner can `setCap`. Then max is a blog with extra steps. Some have no cap at all and still print “max 1B” because the first deck did. Read `mint`, `cap`, `setCap`, and whether those names are on a proxy implementation you have not opened.

TABLE
Integer | Where it lives | Stales when
totalSupply | Token storage | Mint, burn, rebase
max / cap | Code or a slide | Owner setCap, or the slide was always a wish
circulating | A memo | Any labelled wallet moves, or the label was wrong
ENDTABLE

## Crystal Stones as a three-integer drill, not a hymn

Published older figures you may meet: total around 135,000,000, circulating around 104,100,000. This academy’s job is to **re-read `totalSupply` on chain 56** at `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on the day you care, then keep the integer in the claims drawer. Matching a slide is consistency on one number. It is not a mine, not a reason to buy, not tuition. Intermediate remains $10 USDT BEP-20 on checkout.

DIAGRAM
POSTER: one huge number
    split --> totalSupply? (read)
           --> cap? (function or wish)
           --> circulating? (named 0x list + date)
If you cannot split, you cannot cite.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Why circulating cannot be a getter, in one extra beat

A contract can know `totalSupply`. It cannot know which holders you consider “locked” unless those holders are programs that refuse `transfer`. Even then, a program can be upgraded if a proxy sits on it. So circulating is always a memo with a date. Anyone selling you circulating as a protocol primitive is selling a dashboard.

## Say this out loud

- Supply is three integers, not one font size.
- totalSupply is a read; circulating is a memo.
- A pie without addresses is art.
- Crystal Stones figures are a drill, not a buy.
- Tuition is $10 USDT BEP-20 on checkout.

lessons.title: Mint versus burn as a net
lessons.content:
# Mint versus burn as a net

Deflation is a marketing word for a net. A contract can burn one million units in a ceremony and mint two million in the same week. The ceremony is a video. The net is plus one million. Tokenomics that only shows the burn is a selected camera angle.

By “net” this lesson means mint minus burn over a stated window, in the same units, with a date on both sides.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to compute net issuance over a window and refuse a burn party that hides a larger mint.

## Two functions, one arithmetic

On a typical BEP-20, `mint` increases `totalSupply` and credits an address. `burn` (or a send to a true dead address) decreases supply, or at least removes units from addresses that can transfer. A dead address that is actually an EOA the team still controls is not a burn. It is a labelled wallet.

Net over window W = units minted in W minus units burned in W. If mint is 5,000,000 and burn is 2,000,000, net is **+3,000,000**. Calling that week “deflationary” is false. Calling a single burn transaction “the policy” is also false. Policy is the stream.

Read verified source for `mint` access control. If `onlyOwner` can mint, the owner is the policy. If a minter role can mint, the role is the policy. If mint is gone and owner is the zero address and there is no proxy, the remaining policy is whatever burn path still exists — and unlocks, which are not burns.

## Burn-on-transfer is not automatically a net negative

Some contracts take a fee on every transfer and send a slice to a dead address. That looks like automatic deflation. It is not automatic net-negative supply if:

- a minter can print faster than the fee burns,
- most units sit idle (no transfers, no fee),
- the fee can be switched off or set to zero for selected addresses,
- excluded addresses (often owner, pairs, treasury) do not pay the fee, so the burn only hits ordinary holders.

Worked case. Average daily transfers move 1,000,000 units at a 2% burn-on-transfer = 20,000 burned. Owner mints 100,000 the same day. Net **+80,000**. The dashboard that prints only “2% burn” is a camera.

## Dead addresses versus cousin addresses

A well-known burn address (the zero address, or a canonical dead address with no key) is a reasonable burn if units actually arrived there. A random 0x in a tweet labelled “burned forever” is a claim. Check `balanceOf` that address, then ask whether anyone has ever transferred *from* it. If yes, it was never dead.

Crystal Stones homework, when you care: read `totalSupply` at `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on chain 56. If you also track burns, track mints in the same notebook. Do not pay tuition in CST. Checkout is USDT BEP-20.

## Worked refusal

A poster says “50% burned, ultra rare.” You open the explorer. You find a mint to a treasury the week after the burn party. You write both lines. You do not argue in a group chat. You update the memo. This school still does not tell you to buy the dip that the poster invented.

TABLE
Event | Supply effect | What to record
mint(to, amount) | totalSupply up | minter address, date, amount
burn(amount) or send to true dead | totalSupply down or units untransferable | destination, date, amount
fee-on-transfer burn | small, only on moving units | whether excluded addresses skip it
Unlock from vest | circulating up, total unchanged | not a mint, still inventory
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
WINDOW: 7 days
mint   5,000,000
burn   2,000,000
net   +3,000,000   <-- this is the policy that week
A video of the 2,000,000 is not the policy.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
A burn without a mint column is a selected camera. Write both. Date both. Net is the only honest headline.
ENDNOTE

## Two-block arithmetic you can actually do

Pick block A and block B a month apart. Read `totalSupply` at each (explorer historical, or an archive node). Difference is net mint minus burn. Fees that go to an EOA are not burns. Sends to `0xdead` are burns only if that address cannot spend — conventional, not mystical. A “2% burn tax” that routes to a marketing wallet is a transfer, not a burn.

If net is +12% in 30 days, the poster’s “deflationary” is a font. If net is −1% and the owner can still `mint`, next month can reverse it. Snapshot the blocks. Date the memo. Do not argue from a GIF of a flame.

## Burn that does not decrement

`burn(amount)` that decreases `totalSupply` is a true burn. `transfer(dead, amount)` decreases circulating in a dashboard sense if dead cannot spend. If dead is a key someone holds, it is a labelled wallet. Some taxes mint a sibling token and call that a burn. Read the recipient. Read whether `totalSupply` moved.

TABLE
Action | totalSupply | What you write
burn() that decrements | Down | True burn
send to 0x0…dead | Usually unchanged | Costume unless proven unspendable
tax to marketing EOA | Unchanged | Transfer with a nickname
owner mint | Up | Policy, not weather
ENDTABLE

## Why this school will not celebrate a burn

Burns are inventory policy. They are not a price machine. A smaller list can still have a hidden mint, a pause on sells, and a 1% pool. Tokenomics stops at the net. Markets course refuses to turn the net into a candle. Crystal Stones burn language, if you meet it, is a claim: check whether `totalSupply` actually fell, on which days, by how much. Then stop. Do not buy because a number fell.

## Fees to EOAs, restated

A 2% “burn” that lands on a marketing EOA increases that EOA’s `balanceOf`. It does not decrease `totalSupply`. If they later sell, the units return to a pair. Calling that deflation is a mistranslation. Write the recipient 0x. If the recipient is `address(0)` or a proven dead address **and** totalSupply drops or you are explicitly treating dead as removed, say which convention you used.

## Say this out loud

- Deflation is a net, not a ceremony.
- Mint and burn live in the same notebook.
- Fee-on-transfer can still lose to a minter.
- A labelled burn wallet that can send is not dead.
- Unlocks are not burns.

lessons.title: Decimals and poster math
lessons.content:
# Decimals and poster math

Explorers and contracts speak in raw integer units. Humans speak in tokens. The gap is `decimals`. Most BEP-20 tokens use 18, meaning 1 display token is 10^18 raw units. Posters that drop zeros, mix raw with display, or treat 135e18 as “135 tokens” are not doing tokenomics. They are doing typesetting accidents.

This lesson is the arithmetic so you stop trusting a screenshot of a huge integer without asking which scale it used.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to convert raw units to display units with decimals, and catch a poster that mixed the two scales.

## What decimals actually is

`decimals` is a display hint stored in the contract (or assumed by a wallet). The ledger itself is an integer. `balanceOf(alice)` might return 1000000000000000000. With decimals 18, wallets show 1. With decimals 9, the same raw integer is 1,000,000,000 display units. The chain did not change. The caption did.

USDT on BSC is commonly 18 decimals in the BEP-20 wrapping used on this chain; other USDT deployments on other chains have used 6. That is why “USDT” without a chain is an incomplete name. Crystal Stones is taught as a BEP-20 on chain 56. Read `decimals` on the contract you actually opened.

## Poster failure modes

Four common lies, often accidental:

1. **Raw pasted as display.** A writer copies `totalSupply` raw, 1.35e26, and captions it “135 septillion tokens, infinite dump.” With 18 decimals that is 135 million display tokens. The dump story was a decimal error.
2. **Display treated as raw.** A dashboard shows 135,000,000. Someone multiplies by 10^18 again and reports a fantasy cap.
3. **Mixed columns.** A table lists wallet A in raw and wallet B in display. The pie becomes nonsense.
4. **Rounding as policy.** “About 135 million” is not a read. It is a rounded marketing line. Write the integer the function returned.

Worked case. Raw `totalSupply` = 135000000000000000000000000. Decimals = 18. Display = 135,000,000. If a poster says 135,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 “because BscScan showed a long number,” the poster cannot read an explorer.

## Why this matters for Crystal Stones drills

Older Crystal Stones materials may say about 135,000,000 total. Your job is still to read `totalSupply` at `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on chain 56 and divide by 10^decimals yourself. Matching a rounded poster is not the win. Matching the integer on the day you care is the win. Matching is not tuition. Tuition remains $10 USDT BEP-20 on academy checkout. Gas is BNB.

## Worked refusal

A cousin forwards a screenshot: “look how many zeros, this cannot dump.” You ask for decimals and the display conversion. You do the division. You find a ordinary eight-digit display supply. You do not lecture. You write the two columns in your memo and close the thread. This school still assigns no trade.

TABLE
Raw integer | decimals | Display tokens
1 000000000000000000 | 18 | 1
135 000000000000000000000000 | 18 | 135,000,000
135 000000000 | 9 | 135,000,000
135000000 | 0 | 135,000,000
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
READ  totalSupply_raw
READ  decimals_n
DISPLAY = totalSupply_raw / 10^decimals_n
Write DISPLAY with the date.
Do not caption raw as if it were DISPLAY.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Decimals are a caption, not a vault. A long explorer integer without division is not a supply shock.
ENDNOTE

## Raw units versus display units

ERC-20/BEP-20 balances are integers. `decimals()` tells wallets where to put the point. 18 decimals: display 1.0 is 1e18 raw. 6 decimals (USDT-class): display 1.0 is 1e6 raw. Mixing them in a spreadsheet concatenates a fantasy FDV. Always keep a decimals column next to every supply integer.

Worked trap. Token A 18 decimals, totalSupply raw 1e26, display 100,000,000. Token B 6 decimals, totalSupply raw 1e14, display 100,000,000. Same display, wildly different raw. A pie that adds display numbers from two tokens without decimals is not a pie. It is concatenation.

## Why wallets round and posters lie

Wallets round. Explorers shorten. A poster that prints 135M may mean 135,000,000.000000000000000000 or 135,000,000 plus a remainder they dropped. When you compare a slide to `totalSupply`, compare **raw** or compare display with the same decimals and no rounding. “Close enough” is how stale decks survive.

TABLE
Field | Store it as | Failure
decimals | Integer from the contract | Assuming 18
totalSupply raw | Integer | Mixing with a 6-decimal cousin
display | raw / 10^decimals | Rounding in a screenshot
price * supply | Named as market cap or FDV, with the supply you actually used | Mixing circulating and max in one multiply
ENDTABLE

## Academy numbers stay on-chain

This school will not give you a Crystal Stones market cap. If you read `decimals` and `totalSupply` on chain 56, you have two integers and a date. Multiplying by a venue price is markets work this course will not assign. Checkout is still $10 USDT BEP-20, 18 or 6 decimals on **that** USDT contract, not on CST.

## Price × supply, which supply

If a poster multiplies a DEX price by max, they printed FDV. If they multiply by a circulating memo, they printed a headline market cap. If they multiply by totalSupply, they printed something in between. Write which. Do not argue “cheap” until the integer is named. This school still will not call it cheap.

## Say this out loud

- The ledger is raw integers.
- decimals is a display hint.
- Never mix raw and display in one pie.
- Divide by 10^decimals yourself.
- A rounded poster is not a read.

lessons.title: Uncapped, rebase, and elastic stories
lessons.content:
# Uncapped, rebase, and elastic stories

Some tokens have no max. Some change every holder’s balance overnight without a transfer. Some advertise “elastic supply that follows demand.” These are not three words for the same machine. They are three ways a poster can hide a policy. If you only learned max / total / circulating, these designs will look like magic. They are not magic. They are functions.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to distinguish uncapped mint, rebase, and elastic designs, and write what each does to a holder’s units and share.

## Uncapped is a missing ceiling

Uncapped means `totalSupply` can rise without a coded maximum, usually because `mint` still works. It is honest if the page says so. It is a trap if the page prints a “max” that exists only in a PDF. Dilution of share = new mint / (old total + new mint), if you held a fixed balance. Your units may stay 1,000. Your share of the list falls.

Worked case. Total 100,000,000. You hold 1,000,000 (1%). Owner mints 100,000,000 to a treasury. Total is now 200,000,000. You still hold 1,000,000 (0.5%). No transfer appeared in your wallet. The policy did.

## Rebase changes balances in place

A rebase token stores shares or scaling factors. When the contract “rebases up 2%,” many wallets show 2% more units without those wallets sending or receiving a normal transfer. Explorers can look confusing: your `balanceOf` changed, but there is no transfer row you initiated.

Rebasing up is not yield from a warehouse. It is a rescaling of the list. If price per unit falls by about the same factor, you have more units of a smaller claim. If the design rebases down, your displayed units shrink. Either way, **share** may stay constant while **units** move — the opposite of an uncapped mint that prints to someone else.

Write both columns: units and estimated share. Posters that only show unit growth are selling a rescaling as a payday.

## Elastic stories

“Elastic” copy usually means: supply expands when price is high and contracts when price is low, by rebase or by mint/burn against an oracle. The oracle is a data pipe. If the pipe is a pool the team can move, elasticity is a joystick. If there is no oracle, “elastic” is a vibe word for uncapped.

This academy does not assign an elastic trade. It assigns a question: which function runs, who may call it, what oracle it reads, and whether your share is protected. Crystal Stones is not taught here as a rebase token; still read the source the day you care. Verified source is a compiler match, not an audit.

## Worked refusal

A poster: “balances up 5% this week, holders getting paid.” You check: rebase, not a dividend from a company. Price per unit is not in the contract. You write “rescaling, not a coupon.” You do not convert academy XP into this ticker. Ranks in this school are database rows, not tokens.

TABLE
Design | Units in your wallet | Your share of total | Hidden joystick
Capped, no mint | Stable unless you send | Stable unless others mint (they cannot) | Proxy/admin
Uncapped mint to others | Stable | Falls | Minter
Rebase up | Rises | Often stable | Oracle / admin
Elastic via oracle | Moves | Depends | Oracle and caller
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
DAY 0: total 100,000,000  you 1,000,000  share 1.00%
MINT 100,000,000 to treasury
DAY 1: total 200,000,000  you 1,000,000  share 0.50%
REBASE +2% instead:
DAY 1: total 102,000,000  you 1,020,000  share 1.00%
Same word “supply changed.” Two machines.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Uncapped, rebase, and elastic are not synonyms. Write units and share as two columns or you are reading a poster.
ENDNOTE

## Rebase is a balance rewrite, not a transfer

A positive rebase increases `balanceOf` without you receiving a transfer event you initiated. A negative rebase decreases it. If a lending market treats the token as ordinary collateral, a positive rebase can look like extra collateral the borrower did not post. Health ratios lie. This is how “elastic dollar” designs become unsafe when composed. You do not need to use them. You need to see the lie in the mapping.

## Uncapped plus a farm is a firehose

If `mint` has no cap and a farm calls it every block, supply is a faucet. APY screenshots assume the faucet continues and the price of the reward token holds. Tokenomics can only say: mint permission exists, rate is X per block **today**, owner can change rate **if** a setter exists. The rest is a market sentence this school will not write.

TABLE
Design | What balanceOf does | Extra risk
Ordinary capped ERC-20 | Changes on transfer/mint/burn | Owner mint if present
Rebase / elastic | Changes on a supply event | Lending markets misread collateral
Interest-bearing wrapper | Shares vs assets | You must name which integer the poster used
ENDTABLE

## “Algorithmic” is not a third physics

Algorithmic supply is still `mint` and `burn` with a program calling them. If the program’s admin can switch the algorithm, you have a person. If oracles feed the algorithm, you have an oracle. Write those objects. Do not upgrade the word “algorithm” into “cannot fail.”

## Shares versus assets in wrappers

Interest-bearing tokens often track shares internally and assets on a dashboard. A poster that uses the share integer as “supply” understates or overstates depending on the wrapper. Read `convertToAssets` or the equivalent if present. If you cannot, write “wrapper: integer unspecified.” Do not mash it into an ordinary totalSupply row.

## Say this out loud

- Uncapped is a missing ceiling plus a minter.
- Rebase can change units without your transfer.
- Unit growth is not a coupon from a warehouse.
- Elastic without an oracle is a vibe.
- Ranks here are database rows, not tokens.

lessons.title: Cliff and linear vest
lessons.content:
# Cliff and linear vest

Allocations that “belong to the team” are often not in the market yet. They are a calendar: nothing for a while, then a lump, then a drip. The calendar has two named parts. A **cliff** is a period with zero release. A **linear vest** is a drip after the cliff (or from day one) until the allocation is fully transferable. Mixing those words with “locked forever” is how posters hide future inventory.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to draw a cliff-plus-linear schedule in units per month and say what circulating does when the cliff ends.

## Cliff is a delay, not a burn

Cliff = 6 months, allocation = 12,000,000. For six months the 12 million does not arrive in transferable form for that beneficiary — if the vest is real. On the cliff date, either a lump arrives or the linear clock starts. Nothing was destroyed. Units were queued.

If the “cliff” is only a spreadsheet, the beneficiary may already hold the tokens in a hot wallet. A spreadsheet cannot stop `transfer`. A vesting contract can, until it pays.

## Linear vest is a drip

After a 6-month cliff, 18 months linear on 12,000,000 means: at month 6, the clock starts (sometimes a 1/18th lump, sometimes zero lump and a daily drip). Roughly 12,000,000 / 18 ≈ **666,667** display tokens per month become transferable, if the contract is honest and the beneficiary claims.

Circulating, honestly computed, rises as those units become able to `transfer` — whether or not they are sold. Ability to sell is inventory. Sale is a later choice.

Worked path. Months 0–5: released 0. Month 6: first slice. Months 6–23: remaining slices. Month 24: 12,000,000 released. If a poster still subtracts the whole 12 million from circulating in month 20, the poster is lying by about 10 million.

## What a vest is not

Not a promise the beneficiary will hold. Not a promise they will not hedge. Not a lock on a DEX pair. Not a mineral royalty. Not academy XP. A vest is a time function on a list of units.

If there is no contract — only a tweeted calendar — you have a social schedule. Social schedules slip. Code can also slip if an admin can call `release` early, `revoke` silently, or upgrade a proxy.

## Worked refusal

A page says “team tokens locked 2 years.” You ask: cliff length, linear length, contract address, who is beneficiary, who is admin, can they revoke or accelerate. If the answer is a PNG of a Gantt chart, you write “calendar, not code.” You do not treat the PNG as a ceiling on circulating.

TABLE
Month | Released if cliff 6 + linear 18 on 12,000,000 | Still queued
0–5 | 0 | 12,000,000
6 | first slice (~666,667 if even monthly) | ~11,333,333
12 | ~4,000,000 cumulative | ~8,000,000
24 | 12,000,000 | 0
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
TIME ---->
[---- cliff 6 mo ----][======= linear 18 mo =======]
0 released              drip ~666,667 / month
Circulating rises when units become transferable, not when a PNG says “aligned.”
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
A cliff delays inventory. It does not delete it. Linear vest is a drip of the same inventory.
ENDNOTE

## A calendar is not a locker

T+0 mint to locker. T+12 months cliff 25%. Then 24 months linear. That paragraph is a **description**. The locker must encode start, cliff, slope, and beneficiary. If start is a variable the owner can `set`, the calendar is a blog. If there is no locker, only a team EOA, there is no cliff. There is trust, which you may choose; you may not relabel it as code.

## Cliff math, slowly

100 million to a vest. 12-month cliff, then 24 months linear. For 12 months, releasable is 0 (if the code agrees). At cliff, 25 million may unlock as a chunk, or the linear may start from zero depending on the contract — **read which**. Then 75 million over 24 months is about 3.125 million per month if linear in months, or per-second if the contract is honest about time. A PNG that shows a smooth ramp is not the per-second function.

TABLE
Shape | What happens at T_cliff | What happens after
Cliff then linear | Often a chunk, then a trickle | Trickle until end
Pure linear from T0 | Nothing special at month 12 | Trickle from day one
Manual release | Whatever admin calls | Trust
No contract, labelled EOA | Admin mood | Not a vest
ENDTABLE

## Why unlock days are not a “dump switch” this school will press

An unlock is permission to transfer. Whether someone sells is a market question. This course records the permission and the date. It does not tell you to short the unlock. It does not tell you to buy the dip. Empty signal box.

## Per-second versus per-month slides

A slide with twelve monthly bars is not proof the contract pays monthly. Many vests are per-second: the bar is a rounding of a slope. Some only `release` when someone calls it, so the bar is an upper bound until a tx happens. Write “slope is per-second, release is pull” or whatever the code says. Do not cite the bar as bytecode.

## Say this out loud

- Cliff is zero release, not a burn.
- Linear vest is a drip after (or without) a cliff.
- Ability to transfer is inventory.
- A PNG calendar is not a contract.
- Do not subtract fully-vested units as if they were dead.

Next: reading a vest or locker.

lessons.title: Reading a vest or locker
lessons.content:
# Reading a vest or locker

Lockers and vesting contracts are programs. They are not temples. Some are well-used open sources. Some are a three-line contract whose owner can `withdraw` at will. Reading the locker is how you decide whether “locked until 2027” is a function or a caption.

This lesson is a path: find the lock, read beneficiary, amount, unlock time, and admin, then watch whether units actually cannot move before that time.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to inspect a vest or locker for amount, unlock time, beneficiary, and admin overrides, and reject a lock screenshot that omits those four.

## Four fields that make a lock real enough to write down

1. **Amount** — `balanceOf(locker)` today, not a tweeted number from listing day.
2. **Unlock time** — a timestamp in code, or a cliff plus duration. Convert it to a calendar date in your memo. Unix timestamps in posters are often wrong by a year.
3. **Beneficiary** — who receives the units. If it is an EOA the team uses for trading, the unlock is future float into a trading wallet.
4. **Admin** — `owner`, `revoke`, `extend`, `releaseEarly`, proxy admin. An admin who can pull units now means the unlock date is decorative.

If any field is missing, write “lock not evidenced.” Do not write “safe.” Do not write “scam” without the fields; you may simply be unable to see.

## Locker factories versus homemade locks

A widely used locker factory at least has public documentation and a pattern you can compare. Homemade locks fail in boring ways: the token was transferred to an ordinary wallet labelled “TeamLock”; the locker token is a different 0x with the same name; the lock is of LP tokens while the team still holds raw inventory; the lock expired two months ago and nobody updated the website.

Worked case. Website: “10,000,000 locked until 1 Jan 2027.” Explorer: locker holds 2,000,000, owner() is a team EOA, there is `emergencyWithdraw`. You record 2 million, not 10 million, and you record the emergency function. The website can keep its caption. Your memo does not.

## What successful unlock looks like

On unlock, units move from locker to beneficiary. Circulating, honestly computed, should rise by that amount if you had subtracted it. If units move *before* the advertised date, the advertisement was false. If units never sat in the locker, the advertisement was fiction from the start.

Crystal Stones: this school does not publish a live locker table that will be wrong next month. If you care, you read holders on `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` chain 56 and you follow labelled lock addresses the same day. Not a buy. Not tuition.

## Worked refusal

A chat admin pastes a locker UI connected to a clone domain. You do not connect a wallet to “prove the lock.” You open a bookmarked explorer, paste the locker 0x from paper, and read. Connecting to a locker website is how people sign a drain. Reading is free and quieter.

TABLE
Field | Acceptable evidence | Costume
Amount | balanceOf(locker) today | Listing-day PNG
Unlock time | Timestamp in verified source | “Q4 sometime”
Beneficiary | Address in code | “the team”
Admin override | Presence or absence of withdraw/revoke | “trust us”
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
WEBSITE: 10,000,000 locked to 2027-01-01
EXPLORER: locker balance 2,000,000
          owner() = team EOA
          emergencyWithdraw() exists
MEMO: 2,000,000, override possible, date decorative.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
A lock is four fields. A screenshot of a padlock emoji is zero fields.
ENDNOTE

## Function names that mean you are looking at a program

`beneficiary`, `start`, `duration`, `cliff`, `released`, `releasable`, `release`, `vestedAmount`. If those are missing and you are looking at an EOA with a name tag “Team Vesting,” you are looking at a person. Open Write-as-proxy if the 0x is a shell.

`setBeneficiary` means the stream can be redirected. That can be a lost-key safety and a theft feature. Presence is information. Absence plus an EOA holding the tokens is worse: they already have the inventory.

## Revocation and rug-shaped “Vest”

Some vests let the owner `revoke` and return unreleased tokens to the company. That is a real design in employment tokens. On a public meme allocation it means the pie chart can be pulled back. Read `revocable`. A locker that can `withdraw(to, amount)` to owner is not a locker. It is a labelled wallet with extra steps.

DIAGRAM
READ on vest 0x
  beneficiary?
  start / cliff / duration?
  released / releasable?
  owner / setBeneficiary / revoke?
  token 0x (must be the ticker you think)
If token() points at a different BEP-20, the vest is for another list.
ENDDIAGRAM

## LP lockers are a different object

A token vest pays the **ticker**. An LP locker holds **LP tokens** that can `burn` to pull reserves. Confusing them is how people think “renounced + locked” while the LP locker is owner-withdrawable. Two 0x addresses. Two reads. Crystal Stones homework is still verify-only on the token contract, not an assignment to use a locker.

## token() mismatch

Vest contracts point at a token. If `token()` is not the 0x on your memo, the vest is for a different list — a leftover, a test, or a bait. Always read `token()`. LP lockers point at an LP token, which itself points at `token0` and `token1`. Confirm those match the ticker and the quote you think.

## Say this out loud

- Amount, time, beneficiary, admin.
- balanceOf(locker) beats a listing PNG.
- emergencyWithdraw makes the date decorative.
- Do not connect a wallet to prove a lock.
- Unlock is future inventory, not a ritual.

Next: allocations as future inventory.

lessons.title: Allocations as future inventory
lessons.content:
# Allocations as future inventory

Tokenomics pages love pies: team 15%, ecosystem 25%, liquidity 10%, community 50%. A pie is a claim about **who is scheduled to be able to sell**. It is not a moral ranking. “Community” units that sit in a wallet the sponsor controls are inventory. “Team” units that are truly unreleased are also inventory, just dated later. This lesson names allocations as a schedule of future float.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to rewrite a pie as a dated inventory table and refuse labels that are not addresses.

## Labels are not wallets

Every slice must map to one or more addresses, or to a vest that pays addresses. If “ecosystem” is unexplained, it is a drawer the sponsor can open. If “community” is airdrop plus treasury plus rewards, it is three drawers mashed so the pie looks generous.

Ask for: address, current balance, vest or lock if any, who signs. Write “unmapped” when they cannot. Unmapped is a valid cell. It is more honest than “for the people.”

## Future inventory, not a vibe

Worked pie. Total 100,000,000 display tokens.

- Liquidity 10,000,000 in a pair contract today — inventory in a market, can be withdrawn if LP tokens are free.
- Team 15,000,000, cliff 12 months, then 12 months linear — inventory starting month 12.
- Treasury 20,000,000, no vest, EOA — inventory now.
- Rewards 25,000,000, emitted 100,000 per day — inventory as a faucet.
- “Community” 30,000,000, unmapped — treat as sponsor-controlled until proven else.

Circulating today is not 100 million and not 0. It is whatever can transfer now. The pie hid that by using category names instead of dates.

## Double counting

Posters double-count: liquidity is listed as 10% and also as “locked community treasure.” Team is 15% and also “advisors 5%” that were carved from team without shrinking team. Burns are shown as a slice and also subtracted from total. Pick one presentation. If a slice is burned, it is not an allocation. If a slice is in a pair, it is liquidity inventory, not a temple.

Academy XP is not an allocation of CST. Ranks are database rows. Anyone selling “Adept rank for tokens” is not this school.

## Worked refusal

A launch page: 40% community. You ask for the 0x. They send a Discord role screenshot. You write “40% unmapped.” You do not argue that they are evil. You refuse to treat 40% as unavailable float.

TABLE
Slice | Address? | Date it can transfer | Inventory now?
Liquidity 10m | Pair contract | Now, if LP unlocked | Yes, in the curve
Team 15m | Vest | After cliff | No until cliff
Treasury 20m | EOA | Now | Yes
Rewards 25m | Emitter | Daily | Partial
Community 30m | Unmapped | Unknown | Treat as yes
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
PIE LABELS          -->   DATED INVENTORY
community 40%             unmapped 40m  (assume movable)
team 15%                  vest, month 12+
liquidity 10%             pair inventory now
If a slice has no 0x, it is not a slice. It is fog.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
A pie without addresses and dates is a mood board. Rewrite it as inventory by month.
ENDNOTE

## Rows must resolve to addresses

Team 15%, advisors 5%, ecosystem 20%, liquidity 10%, public 50%. Each row should resolve to an 0x or a set of 0x, plus a vest if claimed. “Ecosystem” that sits on an EOA that can move today is circulating, whatever the pie said. “Community” is not an address.

## Investor rounds are permission, not prophecy

SAFTs and unlock tables, when they exist, tell you **who is allowed to sell**, not who will. Tokenomics stops at permission. A round that unlocked last month is inventory that **may** hit a book. This school will not convert that into a short recommendation.

TABLE
Row | Acceptable evidence | Costume
Team | Vest 0x, beneficiary, cliff | “Team 15%” with no address
Liquidity | Pair 0x + locker 0x | “10% LP” in a deployer EOA
Ecosystem | Named contracts or a governor | A founder hot wallet
Public | TGE / claim contract | “Fair launch” plus a 40% insider mint
ENDTABLE

## Pie charts without decimals and without chain ID

A pie that does not name chain ID and token 0x can be a pie of a different contract. Copycats reprint famous pies. Paste the 0x from a bookmark, then see whether the labelled wallets even hold that token. If they hold a lookalike, the pie is theatre.

## Public versus insider, as permission

“Fair launch” plus a 40% insider mint is not a fair launch. It is a mint with a caption. Tokenomics does not need a speech about fairness. It needs the mint amount and the addresses. Write “insider inventory 40%, addresses: …” or “addresses not evidenced.”

## Say this out loud

- Allocations are future or present inventory.
- Labels are not wallets.
- Unmapped community is sponsor float until proven.
- Do not double-count burns and slices.
- XP is not a token allocation.

Next: liquidity is inventory, not a temple.

lessons.title: Liquidity is inventory, not a temple
lessons.content:
# Liquidity is inventory, not a temple

People speak of “the LP” as if it were a shrine that protects holders. Liquidity is units sitting in a pool or on a book so that someone can sell into them. Those units are inventory. If the inventory is thin, a modest sell walks the price. If the LP tokens are free in a team wallet, the inventory can be removed. Neither fact is a moral failing of mathematics. Both are tokenomics.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to describe pool inventory as units that can be bought or withdrawn, and refuse “locked liquidity” without a locker read.

## What a pair holds

On an automated market maker, a pair contract holds two balances: base token and quote token (often a stable or the chain’s native wrapped coin). Those balances are the book. Size is visible: `balanceOf(pair)` for each token. A poster that says “deep liquidity” without those two integers is chanting.

Worked numbers. Pair holds 8,000,000 CST-like units and 80,000 USDT. A seller of 800,000 units is not a rounding error. Impact will be large relative to a seller of 800 units. This school still assigns no size and no pair. It assigns the habit of reading both balances.

## LP tokens are the claim on that inventory

Whoever holds the LP tokens can usually withdraw inventory (burn LP, receive both sides), subject to the pool’s rules. “Liquidity locked” means those LP tokens sit in a locker until a date — if the locker is real. If LP tokens sit in a team EOA, liquidity is a withdrawal away.

Locking LP does not lock the team’s *other* wallets. Raw token inventory outside the pair can still sell into the pair. A 10,000,000 lock of LP plus 40,000,000 free in a treasury is not “10 million float.” It is a thin book with a large potential seller.

## Temple language

“Thank the LP.” “The LP is sacred.” “Don’t dump on the LP.” These are social pressures. The pool will fill whatever order the curve allows. It does not have feelings. Tokenomics literacy is: read inventory, read who can pull it, read who sits outside it with units.

On a central limit book, the analog is size at the inside and behind. A one-tick spread on 200 units is not a temple either. It is 200 units.

## Worked refusal

A listing thread: “LP locked 100 years.” You find a locker of LP tokens for 30 days, or a lock of a different token, or a lock on a testnet. You write the actual amount and date. You do not send CST to “add sacred LP” as homework. You do not pay tuition into a pair. Checkout is USDT BEP-20 on the academy page.

TABLE
Object | What it is | Failure if you worship it
Pair balances | Inventory for swaps | You treat thin balances as a floor
LP tokens | Claim to withdraw inventory | You ignore who holds them
LP locker | Time lock on that claim | You skip emergencyWithdraw
Treasury outside pair | Extra inventory | You subtract it as “locked community”
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
PAIR balances:  8,000,000 token   +   80,000 quote
LP tokens:      team EOA 70%   locker 30% until date D
TREASURY:       40,000,000 token (not in pair)
Inventory that can hit the curve is not “the locked 30%.”
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Liquidity is inventory. A padlock emoji on a pair is not a proof. Read balances and LP holders.
ENDNOTE

## 1% LP, 50% team is a shape, not a moral

If a tiny pool sits next to a large unlocked team wallet, the team can sell into a thin book and the candle will look like a waterfall. Renouncing the **token** contract does not freeze the **LP**. Two different 0x addresses. Token `owner() == 0` while LP sits on an EOA is a costume pair.

## What “locked LP” must mean

LP tokens in a locker whose `withdraw` is impossible until a timestamp, with no owner override, is closer to a lock. LP in a locker with `withdraw` to owner is a labelled wallet. LP in a dead address is a lock of the **LP token**, which is not the same as burning the pool’s underlying — it means nobody can `removeLiquidity` those shares, unless the dead key exists.

TABLE
LP location | Can reserves be pulled? | Honest name
Pair contract itself (not LP in a wallet) | By LP holders via burn | Reserves
Locker, no withdraw until T | After T, by whoever the locker pays | Time lock
Locker, owner withdraw | Yes, by owner | Labelled wallet
Deployer EOA | Yes, now | Unlocked inventory
ENDTABLE

## This school will not grade a pool as “enough”

Depth is a markets number. Tokenomics only names where LP lives and who can pull it. Do not ask Mentor for “is the LP safe to buy into.” That is a desk. The box stays empty.

## Renounce versus LP, one more time as a table you can recite

TABLE
Claim | What you open | What would make it true
Token renounced | owner() and roles on token | No minter, no pauser, no proxy admin
LP locked | LP token holder, locker code | No withdraw until T, no owner override
Pool deep | Reserves versus your size | Markets object — not this course’s grade
ENDTABLE

## Say this out loud

- Pair balances are the book.
- LP tokens pull inventory.
- Locked LP is only as good as the locker.
- Treasury outside the pair is still inventory.
- Do not pay tuition into a pool.

Next: Module 3 — taxes, treasuries, emissions.

modules.description: Transfer taxes, treasury keys, emission flows, points versus tokens.

lessons.title: Transfer taxes
lessons.content:
# Transfer taxes

A transfer tax is a cut taken when units move: to a treasury, to holders, to a dead address, or to an address the author did not describe. Ordinary BEP-20 transfers move the full amount. Taxed tokens do not. If you send 100 units and the receiver gets 95, the tax was 5, and the missing 5 went somewhere. Tokenomics that hides the somewhere is incomplete. Tokenomics that hides the *switch* is dangerous.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to trace a taxed transfer from sender amount to receiver amount and name where the gap went, including the switch risk.

## The gap is the lesson

Worked case. You sign a transfer of 100.00 display tokens. Receiver `balanceOf` rises by 95.00. Pair or router might show 92.00 after slippage on top. Separate those. Tax is a contract rule. Slippage is a curve.

Where did 5.00 go? Split example: 2.00 to a “marketing” EOA, 2.00 to a dead address, 1.00 to holders as a reflection. You now have three destinations. Marketing EOA is inventory for whoever holds that key. Dead is a burn if truly dead. Reflection is a rebase-like credit to others.

Read `transfer` / `_transfer` in verified source. Look for `require` on max tx, max wallet, and `excludeFromFee`. Excluded addresses — often owner, pair, and friends — do not pay. The tax then falls on ordinary holders only. That is a policy.

## Taxes that change

A constant 5% is one object. A variable `taxFee` the owner can set to 25% is another. A “honeypot” pattern is an extreme: sell tax 99%, buy tax 0%, or a blacklist. You will meet switches in Module 5. Here, write: current buy tax, current sell tax, current transfer tax, who can change them, and whether DEX pairs are treated differently from wallet-to-wallet.

Routers complicate reads: a “sell” is a transfer to a pair. If only transfers *to* the pair are taxed at the high rate, holders can still wallet-transfer cheaply and sells are gated. That is still a tax policy.

## What a tax is not

Not a government levy. Not academy tuition. Not gas. Gas on BSC is **BNB**, paid to validators, even if the token taxes you. Not proof of backing. A 10% tax does not mean 10% of a mine moved.

Do not send CST to “reduce your tax tier.” This school’s checkout is $10 USDT BEP-20. A Mentor message that asks you to approve a tax-optimizer contract is a malfunction.

## Worked refusal

A poster: “2% tax fuels the ecosystem.” You find `setTax` unbounded, currently 2, and `excludeFromFee` on ten addresses. You write “2% for some, 0% for others, switch exists.” You do not celebrate the ecosystem. You have a policy memo.

TABLE
Leg | 100 sent | Notes
Receiver gets | 95 | Display units
Marketing EOA | 2 | Inventory for that key
Dead address | 2 | Burn only if truly dead
Reflection | 1 | Other holders’ balances
Owner setTax | ? | If unbounded, 95 is temporary
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
SEND 100
  |-- 95 to receiver
  |-- 2  to marketing EOA
  |-- 2  to dead
  +-- 1  reflection
ASK: who is excluded? who can setTax? buy vs sell vs transfer?
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
A tax is a gap plus a destination plus a switch. Missing any of the three is an incomplete read.
ENDNOTE

## Sell-only tax is a cousin of a honeypot

Code like `if (to == pair) fee = high` means exits are taxed harder than entries. At 99% it is a honeypot. At 20% it is still a gap you must include. A “fair 2%” that `setFee` can raise to 99 is a delayed honeypot. Read the setter, the max bound, and who is `excludedFromFee`.

## How a tax breaks allowances and routers

Some taxed tokens break ERC-20 expectations: `transfer` sends less than `amount`, so routers revert, or `balanceOf` after a transfer is not what a naive integrator expected. Integrations fail; users think “the DEX is down.” The token is the unusual object. If you cannot sell through the ordinary router, that is information, not a reason to run a random “tax-optimizer” approval.

DIAGRAM
transfer(amount)
   --> maybe fee to marketing / burn / LP
   --> recipient gets amount - fee
Routers that assume amount-in = amount-out will mis-price or revert.
ENDDIAGRAM

TABLE
Question | Why it matters
Can owner setFees with no cap? | 2% is temporary
Is pair excluded? | Owner can sell untaxed
Does approve/transferFrom match ERC-20? | Routers may fail
Is there a maxTx or cooldown? | Exit is throttled
ENDTABLE

## maxTx, cooldown, and the slow exit

Some tokens cap how much you can sell per transaction or per block. Combined with a tax, exit is a trickle. That is still a tokenomics door. It is not “the market dumped me.” Read `maxTxAmount`, `cooldown`, `antiBot`. Anti-bot that never turns off is a throttle on you.

## Say this out loud

- Receiver amount is the first measurement.
- Name where the gap went.
- excludeFromFee is part of the policy.
- Tax is not gas and not tuition.
- An unbounded setTax is a joystick.

Next: treasury versus community.

lessons.title: Treasury versus community
lessons.content:
# Treasury versus community

Two words share a poster and rarely share a key. **Treasury** is an address (or a set) that holds units and, in a serious design, has rules for spending. **Community** is a social word: chat, holders, “the people.” If community units live in the same EOA as treasury, you have one wallet with two captions. Tokenomics is about keys, not captions.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to separate treasury addresses from community slogans, and grade a spend as documented, discretionary, or invisible.

## Treasury as a key

A treasury you can write down has: one or more addresses, a current `balanceOf`, a signer story (EOA, 3-of-5 multisig, timelock), and a purpose. Purpose without a signer is a blog post. Signer without a purpose is a pile.

Worked numbers. Total 100,000,000. Treasury EOA holds 12,000,000. Multisig holds 3,000,000 labelled operations. “Community rewards” are 8,000,000 in the same EOA as treasury. You do not have 8 million community. You have 20 million under two keys, 12 + 8 mashed on the pie.

## Discretion versus policy

Documented spend: a published policy (“we sell at most 50,000 a week to pay vendors”) plus on-chain history that roughly matches. Discretionary: the key can send anything any day. Invisible: you cannot find the address.

None of these is automatically evil. Discretionary treasuries run many companies. You just stop calling them “community-owned.” A timelock that delays spends is a real constraint. A Discord poll that the signer can ignore is theatre.

## Community as a mash-up

Holders of a transferable token are not a cooperative unless law and documents say so. They cannot force a dividend. They cannot force an audit. They can sell, hold, or talk. That is not nothing. It is not a board seat.

This academy’s community features — chat with Mentor, ranks, certificates — are school objects. They are not a claim on a treasury of CST. Certificates are academic. Checkout does not fund a mineral SPV.

## Worked refusal

A campaign: “community treasury will buy the floor.” You find a single EOA, no timelock, no policy. You write “discretionary wallet, slogan attached.” You do not place a floor-buy order because a slogan told you to. This course still has an empty signal box.

TABLE
Label | What would make it real | Costume
Treasury | Address, balance, signer, purpose | A pie slice named treasury
Multisig | On-chain threshold, named signers | “We are a DAO” with one EOA
Timelock | Delay in code | A promise to wait
Community | Addresses or a legal coop | A chat role
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
PIE: community 40%   treasury 12%
KEYS: one EOA holds both piles (20m + mashed remainder)
MEMO: one key, two captions.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
If two captions share a key, you have one treasury. Community is not a signer.
ENDNOTE

## 2-of-3 is three people, not holders

A treasury multisig is better than one EOA. It is not a Governor. Holders do not vote it unless a governor’s `execute` is the only spender. Do not upgrade the label because the UI says “community treasury.”

## Spending that needs two keys still spends

If 2-of-3 can send 100% of the bag, the bag is theirs. A policy PDF that says “max 2% per month” is a blog unless the contract enforces it. Read `transfer` rights, not the PDF.

TABLE
Control | Honest name | Still a person?
EOA owner | Company wallet | Yes
Multisig | Several people | Yes
Timelock + EOA | Delay, then a person | Yes
Governor + timelock | Holders who bother to vote, if weight is real | Weight, not magic
ENDTABLE

## Academy treasury is not this object

This school’s tuition in USDT is an invoice. It is not a DAO bag you vote. Mixing academy checkout with a protocol treasury is how impersonators invent a “governance payment.” Checkout stays on the academy origin. CST stays verify-only.

## How to read a treasury without a tour

On an explorer, the treasury is an address with a token balance. Open it. Is it a contract? If EOA, one key. If multisig, open the module and count owners and threshold. If a governor timelock, read `delay` and `admin`. Write those four facts on the memo. A UI that says “owned by the community” while the 0x is an EOA is a mistranslation.

Worked split. 40 million of a ticker sit on 0xAAA labelled treasury. 0xAAA is a 2-of-3. The three owners are EOAs that also hold team allocation. Then “community treasury” is three team keys with extra steps. Not evil by itself. Not holder control. Do not upgrade the noun.

## Forum vote then EOA send

A temperature check passes. An EOA sends the bag. The government is the EOA. The vote was a blog. You will meet this again in DAOs. Tokenomics only needs you to notice that the spender 0x is what matters, not the poll screenshot.

## Say this out loud

- Treasury is an address plus a signer.
- Community is not automatically a key.
- Discretionary spend is allowed to exist; do not rename it.
- Timelocks constrain; polls may not.
- Academy ranks are not a claim on a treasury.

Next: emissions are inflation with a dashboard.

lessons.title: Emissions are inflation with a dashboard
lessons.content:
# Emissions are inflation with a dashboard

Staking APY, play-to-earn faucets, liquidity mining, “learn and earn” coins — these are often the same machine: a contract mints or releases units on a schedule to whoever sits in a pool. The dashboard prints a percentage. The list grows. If demand for the units does not grow with the list, price per unit is doing arithmetic you were not shown. This lesson names emissions as inflation with a UI.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to convert an APY screenshot into units per day and say what that does to totalSupply or circulating.

## APY is a rate; emission is a flow

A dashboard showing 120% APY does not tell you how many units leave the faucet tomorrow. Two pools can show the same APY with wildly different unit flows depending on how many people have staked.

Worked case. Emitter pays 100,000 tokens per day, fixed, split pro-rata among stakers. If 1,000,000 is staked, that is 10% of the staked pile per day — an explosive headline APY. If 100,000,000 is staked, it is 0.1% per day. The faucet did not become virtuous. The denominator grew.

Ask for: units per day (or per block), who can change the rate, whether units are minted (totalSupply up) or paid from a prefilled treasury (circulating up, total unchanged), and whether the paid units can sell into the same pair that the farmers use.

## Inflation is not a slur

Some designs emit to pay for security or work. The honest version publishes the flow and the purpose. The dishonest version hides the mint behind “rewards” and a glowing percentage. Your job is the flow. Purpose is a separate sentence.

If mint is 100,000 a day and burn is 5,000 a day, net is +95,000. Module 1 already taught the net. Emissions are how that mint is branded as a gift.

## Dashboards that are not the contract

The UI can lie: show APY on a 7-day window that will not continue, show USD value of rewards using a price the pool cannot bear, show “your rewards” that require a harvest tax of 50%. Read the emitter. Harvest is a transaction. It costs gas in **BNB** on BSC. It may cost a tax. It is not academy XP.

This school will not tell you to farm Crystal Stones. If you verify the contract, you verify. You do not harvest as homework.

## Worked refusal

A poster: “4,000% APY, sustainable.” You ask units per day and the mint function. They send a screenshot of a dashboard. You write “rate without a flow.” You refuse the word sustainable until both columns exist. You still place no farm.

TABLE
Question | Why it matters
Units per day | APY hides the flow
Mint vs treasury pay | totalSupply vs circulating
Who sets the rate | Joystick
Harvest tax / lock | The APY is not take-home
Can rewards sell into the same pool | Reflexive dump path
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
FAUCET: 100,000 units / day
staked 1,000,000   -> headline looks enormous
staked 100,000,000 -> headline shrinks
FLOW DID NOT CHANGE. Denominator did.
Net = mint - burn still wins the week.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
An APY without units-per-day is a costume. Emissions are a flow. Write the flow.
ENDNOTE

## Rate, token, and who can change it

Read `rewardRate` or per-block mint. If the owner can set it, APY is a blog. If the reward token is the same as one side of the pool, you are being paid in the asset the pool is selling into. If 5% of max prints per month to farms, FDV math must include that firehose. A 12-month farm can mint 60% extra.

## Dashboard APY is not a promise

APY annualises a recent rate. If the rate is a week old and the owner cut emissions, the dashboard is a ghost. If the reward token’s book is 1% deep, selling the reward is the real rate, and tokenomics cannot compute your fill. Stop at: inflation permission, current rate, setter, reward 0x.

DIAGRAM
mint --> farm --> user sells reward into pool
                 --> price of reward is a markets object (empty box)
tokenomics only names the mint permission and the rate today
ENDDIAGRAM

## Per-block mint, translated into a month

If a farm mints 10 tokens per block and the chain is ~3 seconds per block, that is 10 × 1,200 × 24 × 30 ≈ 8.64 million per 30-day month, before any setter changes the rate. Put that integer next to totalSupply. If totalSupply is 50 million, a month of farm is not a rounding error. Dashboards that show “APR 2,400%” without this integer are a screenshot of a firehose.

If the reward token is illiquid, the firehose is also a sale into a 1% pool. Tokenomics names the mint. Markets names the fill. This course stops at the mint.

## Say this out loud

- APY is a rate; emission is units per day.
- The same faucet looks calmer when more is staked.
- Minted rewards raise totalSupply.
- Harvest is a transaction, not XP.
- This school assigns no farm.

Next: points are not tokens.

lessons.title: Points are not tokens
lessons.content:
# Points are not tokens

Seasons, quests, leaderboards, “gems,” academy XP, airdrop points — these can live in a company database without any BEP-20 existing. People still sell them in group chats, screenshot them as wealth, and treat them as circulating supply. They are not circulating supply. They are rows. This lesson is the split that saves you from buying a spreadsheet.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to separate points, IOUs, and tokens, and refuse a grey-market points deal as if it were a BEP-20 transfer.

## Three objects

**Points** — a database row at a company or a school. The company can freeze, reset, or multiply them. You cannot `transfer` on a public explorer unless they built that. Crystal Web3 Academy XP and ranks are this object. They are not CST.

**IOU** — a company promises to deliver tokens later. The promise can be broken, delayed, or diluted by changing the conversion rate (10 points = 1 token becomes 100 points = 1 token).

**Token** — a mapping on a chain. Crystal Stones as taught here: BEP-20 at `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on chain 56. Transfer is a signed transaction if the contract allows it.

A season that “converts points to tokens at TGE” is points plus an IOU plus, later, maybe a token. Grade each day of that sentence separately.

## Why grey markets form

If a chat believes points will be tokens, someone will buy points for cash. They are buying a row they do not control, often against terms of service, often with no contract. When the conversion rate moves, they discover they bought a slogan.

Worked numbers. 50,000 points advertised as “worth” a fantasy cash figure. Conversion unpublished. Supply of points uncapped because the quest board can print more. You cannot read `totalSupply` of points on BscScan. There is no such function.

## Academy rails, said again because mash-ups kill

Intermediate is $10 USDT BEP-20 on academy checkout. XP is not a payment. Ranks are not minted. Certificates are academic. Staff never ask for a seed to “sync your points on-chain.” Anyone who needs your seed is an impostor. Gas is BNB. CST is verify-only.

## Worked refusal

A stranger: “I will send you Adept rank if you send USDT.” Ranks are database rows this school computes from study. You do not buy them. You report the message. You do not argue tokenomics with a vendor of rows.

TABLE
Object | Lives where | Can the explorer show it?
XP / rank | Academy database | No
Season points | Sponsor database | No
IOU / allocation sheet | Spreadsheet or app | No
BEP-20 token | Chain (e.g. BSC 56) | Yes, balanceOf
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
POINTS 50,000  -->  IOU (conversion unpublished)  -->  maybe TOKEN at TGE
Each arrow can break.
Academy XP stops at the database. It does not become CST as homework.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Points are rows. Tokens are mappings. Selling ranks is not this academy.
ENDNOTE

## Why this academy’s XP is called XP

If we called ranks a token, someone would sell them. They are rows in a database plus a UI. A DM selling “Adept NFT” or “governance of Crystal Stones Academy” is impersonation, not a TGE of this school. Certificates are academic. They are not BEP-20s.

## Points programs that later “convert”

Off-chain points that later become a mint are a promise plus a future `mint`. The conversion ratio, the cap, and who is excluded live in a future contract that may not exist yet. Treat points as a blog until a contract 0x exists and you have read `mint`. Do not pre-pay a stranger for a conversion.

TABLE
Object | Lives where | Can it be sold on a pair?
XP / rank | Academy DB | No (if someone offers, impersonation)
Off-chain points | Company DB | Not until a token exists
BEP-20 | Chain | If a pair exists — still not homework
ENDTABLE

## Conversion bait, decoded

A site says your academy XP or a project’s points will “convert 1:1 at TGE.” There is no 0x yet. Conversion is a future mint permission plus a list of who is included. Lists get edited. Ratios get edited. A wallet connect to “register points” that requests `approve` on USDT is not registration. Decode the spender. This academy will never convert XP into CST or into USDT. Ranks stay rows.

## Off-chain points plus a connect button

If registering points requires `eth_sign` of a login, that may be a session. If it requires `permit` or `approve` on USDT, it is a gun. Points cannot live in USDT allowance. Decode. This academy login is email-and-password (or the academy’s own session), not a token approve.

## Say this out loud

- XP and ranks are database rows.
- Points can be reset by the operator.
- An IOU conversion rate can move.
- Explorer cannot see a spreadsheet.
- Do not buy Adept from a stranger.

Next: Module 4 — how to read a tokenomics page.
